title: Quiz: Parametric Survival Models and Accelerated Failure Time

questions.text: In a Weibull survival model with shape parameter k = 2, the hazard h(t):
options: Follows a log-normal pattern, first increasing then decreasing
questions.explanation: For the Weibull distribution, h(t) = kλ(λt)^{k−1}. When k > 1, the factor (λt)^{k−1} grows as t increases, so h(t) is strictly increasing. When k = 1 (exponential), h(t) = λ (constant). When k < 1, h(t) is decreasing. Option (d) describes the log-normal hazard, which is unimodal.

questions.text: In an AFT model, a time ratio of φ = 1.8 for a treatment covariate (0 = control, 1 = treated) means:
options: Treated patients have a hazard 1.8 times that of control patients
Treated patients survive 1.8 times as long as control patients on average
The treatment reduces the risk of the event by 80%
On average, 1.8 fewer patients die in the treated group
questions.explanation: In the AFT model, the time ratio φ = exp(β) multiplies the expected survival time. φ = 1.8 means treated patients survive 1.8 times as long as control patients. This is a direct statement about time (the outcome scale), not the hazard scale. Option (a) confuses the time ratio with a hazard ratio. Option (c) would correspond to a hazard ratio of 0.20, not a time ratio.

questions.text: The Weibull model is both a proportional hazards model and an accelerated failure time model — it belongs to the intersection of the two model families.
questions.explanation: The Weibull is the only standard survival distribution that is simultaneously a PH model (h(t|X) = h₀(t)·exp(β_PH′X)) and an AFT model (log T = β₀ + β_AFT′X + σε). The two parameterisations are related by β_PH = −k·β_AFT where k is the Weibull shape parameter. The exponential model (Weibull with k=1) is also in both families. All other standard distributions (log-normal, log-logistic) are AFT models but not PH models.

questions.text: AIC = −2·logL + 2p. When comparing four parametric survival models (exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic) fitted to the same dataset, we prefer the model with:
options: The AIC equal to the number of parameters p
questions.explanation: AIC balances model fit (−2·logL, which decreases as fit improves) against complexity (2p, which penalises additional parameters). A lower AIC indicates a better trade-off between fit and parsimony. The AIC scale is arbitrary — there is no meaningful reference value of 0. What matters is the relative difference between models on the same data.

questions.text: The likelihood ratio test statistic Λ = 2(logL₁ − logL₀) follows an approximate χ² distribution under H₀ when the two models are nested (model 0 is a restricted version of model 1).
questions.explanation: This is Wilks' theorem: under H₀ and regularity conditions, the LRT statistic Λ = 2(logL₁ − logL₀) converges in distribution to χ²(df₁ − df₀), where df₁ − df₀ is the difference in the number of estimated parameters. For example, comparing the Weibull (2 parameters: shape and scale) to the exponential (1 parameter: rate only), the LRT has df = 1. The approximation improves with sample size.
